pages.text: --- Page 1 --- E;NSETE GLAUCUM (ROXB.) CHEESM..IN THE XHASI HILLS, MEGHALAYA, INDIA The genus Ensete Horan., for long, treat- cd under the well known genus Musa L. (and even now so, in some Floras) was resti- tutecl by Cheesman who justified it on the basis of species of E~tsete being monocarpic, with distinctly swollen base, the spathes per- sistent, and the chromosome number, 2n = I 8, being different from that in Musu, 2n = 22 or 20. Although, earlier, Cheesman transferred nulnerous species of Musa to Ensete, later, Simmonds limited ollly six spe- cies in Afri,ca & Asia, of which two occur in India-E. superbnm (Roxb.) Cheesm. and E. glaucum (Roxb.) Cheesm. However, Roxburgh orig'nally described M. glauca from plants introduced into the Company's botanic garden (now the Indian Botanic Garden) from Pegu, Burma, then part of the Indian Empire. The subsequent record of its natural occurrence in India has been doubtful, all the plants seen heing in gar- dens' or nurseries in the North Eastern Re- gion. Hence, Simmonds attributed its oc- currence in India 'probably in Assam'. Apart from the uncertainty of its distribu- tion, he also remarked that only 'a general though still incomplete account of Ensete in Asia' could he given. In drafting an account of the monocot families to complete the hitherto incomplete Kanjilal's Flora of Assam, the family Musa- ceae posed difficnlties due to unsatisfactory col!ections making it necessary to bring to- gether adequate material from different parts of the N. region (the former Assam Region). In this context, a fine inflorescence of what was obviously Ensete glaucum ex- hibited in the Shillong Flower Show in 1968, attractedl our attention, but unfortunately no data as to its source could be obtained, as the exhibitor, an unlettered Khasi farmer had himself obtained it from somebody else. 7 Date of receipt : 12.10.73. Datc of acceptance : 25.3.78. Prcsunlably it was from a kitchen garden. From then onwards a careful watch was kept, and oti 20th June, 1973 a fi~llgroml plant of E. glartct~ was spotted in the front yard of a Khasi farmer, in the village Urn- dihar near Nongpoh. Enquiries revealed that it was a tive year oId plant which he bad raised from seed gathered from the jungle and that he grew it for the sake of its edible soft inner pseudosteul. Subsequ- ently, he guided us to the jungle location, where several scattered plants of various ages were seen naturally growing, near a stream, on a gentle slope. Some more were subsequently spotted in the vicinity of Nongpoh. Further a few plants in full bloom were also discovered in the Barnihat Orange Research Station, and enquiries re- vealed that these were raised from the par- ent plant wh;ch itself had grown from seeds obtained from the Garo Hills, undoubtedly the same material, about which Simmonds has remarked. T h i ~ discovery of Ensete glaucum natu- rally occurring in the forests of the Khasi Hills, coacl~osively establishes its distribu- tion in the N. Region of India (Old Assam). Plants were introduced into the EX- perimental Gardens at "Woodlands" in Shil- lonq and at Barapani. Subba Rao, G. Kumal*i, (in Bull. Surv. India 14 : I 64-1 66. I 972) have reported Ensete glaucum as a relict species in the Eastern Ghats of India, and provided a description. However, considering that this plant is poorly known, and the description is based on plants from that part of the country, it is felt useful to provide a comprehensive description, based on our detailed field observations, supplement- ed by photographs of various parts of the plant, not amenable to treatment by usual herbarium procedures.

Here, it may be re- levant to quke from G. Argent: The Wild  anan an as of Pap~~a New Guincn, in --- Page 2 --- Notes Roy. Bot Gard. Edinburgh 35(1): 77-1 14. 1976-'Bananas are difficult to collect as adequate hcrbarium specimens and re- presentation in herbaria will probably re- main poor ; photographs and accurate field notes almost always carry more taxonomic irzformation than dried herbarium material. ~ l t h o u ~ h pickled specimeils are quite useful and ripe seed samples can be diagnostic, field observation is of paramount importance - in the study of these plants' (underlining ours). The detailed description furnished here is based on field observation of many plants, and together with the photographic illustrations should help in a dearer under- standing of these plants. A reference may also be made to Chakra- vorti'sf Notes on the genus Musa L. in India, and his new species Musn agharkarii from the Chittagong hill tracts. Our study has led us to conclude that M. agharkarii is only Ensete glaucum, and accordingly we have put it in synonymy. Ensete ~laucamrc (Roxb.) Cheesm. in Kew Bull. 1948 ; Simmonds in Kew Bull. Corms shallow, encircled at the top by stout rope like roots 3 q o cm long. Pseudostem 2-4 m tall, distinctly swollen, conical and ridged at base, cylindri- cal and narrow kt top, white pruinose, drap- ed in old leaves in various stages of shrivel- ling up and decay, the stem 3-4 dm in diam. at base, 2-2.5 dm about the middle and I- 1.5 dm at top. Sap bright orange when fresh, turning a dirty grey to black after considerable ' time. Leaf-sheat hs glaucous ahaxially, pinkish-brown adaxially at the point of its divergence from the pseudostern. P~/ioles stout, green-glaucous, I 0-45 cin long: Lamina oblong, 1-2.5 m long, 0.30- 0.60 m broad, the margin entire, rimmed by a thin narrow (ca 2 mnl) menlbrance at first white opaque and in age becoming bIack, the apex acute (caudate in young leaves), the lamina cut up into several seg- ments along the nerves, in age. Flag leaf much smaller than other leaves, 70-75 cm long, 30-35 cm broad (the midrib quite pro- minent).

Inflorescence pendulous, cylindric, large, '-1.5 m long. Spathes several, the basal ones loosely and the apical ones close- ly imbricate, entire, -ovate to ovate-lanceo- late, acute, persistent, green, except the api- cal ones which are sometimes white ; those at base 6-9 empty, with no flowers, subse- quent onesr (up to about half the length, 15- 25 hands) with female flowers, followed by male bisexual flowers up to the tip ; spathes at Inflorescence-base larger, progressively di- minishing in size towards the apex, 20- 35 cm long, 10-20 cm broad. Female flowers 13-24 per hand in rows. Male bisexual flowers numerous, the zone easily recognis- ed by the gradually drying up spathes.. Tepals, the 3 outer united at base 2-2,s cm long with 2 additional linear lobes 1.5- 2.5 cm long, the 2 inner united, with a medi- an furrow, 1-1.2 cm long, with a median mucro, white, becoming shrivelled, black and persistent in fruit. Stamen in female flowers varying from 5 fully formed stamen to 5 filiform staminodes, persistent in fruit ; in male bisexual flowers, of 5 fertile stamens, white, 3-3.5 cm long, the filaments 2 cm long, the anthers I .5-2.0 cm long. Ovary 3-5 cm long, 5-angled, the placenta axiIe, with 3 linear rows of numerous ovule. Style, in female flowers 2-3 cm long, persist- ent in 'fruit ; in male flowers quite .small-ca I cm ; stigrvta in female flowers large, fri- lobed ; in male bisexual flowers inconspicu- ous. Fpuits ovoid to. oblong-ovoid (ar odd- shaped due to pressure while - developing within the spathe), 13-24 fingers p& hand, , green,. turning yellow to irregularly brown: --- Page 3 --- ish yellow at maturity and ultirnattlp b?ack, ish-whitla Seeds black, p r ~ o per fruit, gt* uniformly plump and smooth when fresh, bose to assymynically subg?obote, smooth becoming uneven on drying, 6.5-12 crn long, to vcrp faintly granular, large, ca t cm ac- 1.e3.5 cm across ; pulp scanty fainrly pink- mss, 6 t h a deeply depressed hilum. (5, 10 & 12 from Hqh 45689, r a t rn A. 3, Rm4S684). --- Page 4 --- bryo minute ; endos,perm white, powdery. (Figs. Frequent, on gentle west facing hill slope, beside stream, near lar e boulders, amidst Terminalia, Bauhinia, &. icrcs and Sterculia and with other wild Musa species. Flower- ing and Fruiting, June-August. The mature infrutescence is heavily infested with black an:s. While in the ovary the numerous ovules are in a neat row and embedded in the fleshy pulp, during development in!o fruit the large seeds become irregular, mask- ing the original placentation. The local Khasi. (Bhoi) name is 'Kyiet myntan'. En- quiries showed that the vernacular names (Ram Kal, Aclumatong) kiven by Simmonds referred only to small seed-bearing true bananas and not to Ensete. Occasionally cultivated for its impressive inflorescence, and the soft rind within the pseudostem which is used as a vegetable. Seedlings introduced into the experimental Gardens at Shil'ong and at Barapani are doing well.

During these tours about zoo0 field numbers of plants were collected, which after critical identification, yielded about goo species be- longing to 525 genera under 120 families. These specimens are preserved in the her- barium of Central Circle, Botanical Survey of India, Allahabad (BSA). Besides the~e --- Pate of receipt; 25.12.75. Date of acceptance: 18.10.77. collections, a large number of plant specieg collected earlier from Bilaspur and other districts of Madhya Pradesh are also pre- served there. A review of the literature shows that a few species, hitherto unreport- ed from Madhya Pradesh, are found to oc- m r in this area. Hence their presence in Madhya Pradesh, an entirely distinct phy- togeographical region, is of interest, as it extends considerably their known range of distribution in India. In two earlier com- municatians the author (Murti 1975) report- ed four new records of sp'ecies from Madhya Pradesh viz., Chirita bifolia I). Don, Styli- dizrm kunthii Wall. ex Nees, Althea ludwi gii L. and Lepidagathis purpuricau?is WaU. ex Nees. In the present paper a few more new recoids of species are reported. Following is the account 0% new records of species from Madhya Pradesh. The species are arranged alphabetically. The import- ant diagnostic features are appended with the species enumlrated. The distribution- al notes are from Nook, f . Brit.
